purpose: Simple read-only educational routing based on what visitors know, not their personal medical records
privacy: No text intake; no identifiers; never submit case information

choices.label: I only have a question
choices.sub: I'm curious but don't know the science words yet.

options.label: Show me a discovery story
options.why: A short, sourced story teaches the basics before any searching.
options.action: Read one story. Write down the question that made the scientists curious.
options.caution: A story explains a finding; it isn't proof that the same idea works in a different case.

options.label: Find what scientists have published
options.why: PubMed helps you find research papers and summaries by topic.
options.action: Open PubMed. Search two or three words about your question. Find one paper's title, date, and study type.
options.caution: One paper may be preliminary or contradicted; a published abstract is not a medical recommendation.

choices.label: I know a condition
choices.sub: A health condition or disease name.

options.label: Which genes are linked to it?
options.why: Open Targets collects research evidence connecting diseases and genes.
options.action: Use the disease name to find a disease profile. Look for a linked gene and check what kind of evidence supports it.
options.caution: Linked genes are not necessarily causes or drug targets. Do not enter personal health details.

options.label: What clinical studies exist?
options.why: ClinicalTrials.gov lists publicly registered studies and eligibility information.
options.action: Search the condition, then open one study and find its status, eligibility, location and last update date.
options.caution: A listed trial does not mean it is recruiting, suitable, proven effective or medically recommended.

choices.label: I know a gene
choices.sub: A name like BRAF, TP53, or INS.

options.label: Where is it active in the body?
options.why: The Human Protein Atlas shows where genes and proteins are found in different tissues.
options.action: Search the gene symbol, open its normal-tissue information, and note one tissue with documented expression.
options.caution: Expression does not prove a disease cause or predict treatment safety.

options.label: Do cancer models need it to grow?
options.why: DepMap includes experiments that disable genes in laboratory cancer cell lines.
options.action: Find the gene in DepMap. Look for gene-effect data and the cell-model context before comparing values.
options.caution: A cell-line result is not a response prediction for a person. Some functions need extra statistical knowledge.

choices.label: I know a molecule or drug
choices.sub: A chemical, medicine, or lab compound.

options.label: What exactly is this substance?
options.why: PubChem gives chemical names, structures, identifiers and linked scientific information.
options.action: Search the substance, open its compound page, and note its exact name and compound ID.
options.caution: A chemical profile is not proof of effectiveness or safety; compounds with similar names can differ.

options.label: What lab activity has been reported?
options.why: ChEMBL collects published bioactivity measurements for molecules and biological targets.
options.action: Search a compound name. Open a reported activity and look for the assay type and measured value.
options.caution: Lab activity is not the same as clinical benefit; check assay conditions and licenses.

choices.label: I want to explore an image
choices.sub: A microscope image or research scan.

options.label: Find public images I can study
options.why: TCIA provides collections of imaging data shared for cancer research.
options.action: Browse a public collection. Record the modality, dataset description, and access terms.
options.caution: Never upload someone’s private scan to a public repository or chat.

options.label: Learn how to view a 3D scan
options.why: 3D Slicer is a free desktop program for exploring and analyzing medical images.
options.action: Open Slicer's beginner documentation and find an example dataset and viewing tutorial.
options.caution: This software requires a compatible computer; interpreting clinical scans requires qualified review.

choices.label: I want to explore experiments
choices.sub: Data, cell models, or virtual experiments.

options.label: Find results from published experiments
options.why: NCBI GEO stores public gene-expression and other functional-genomics datasets.
options.action: Search for a topic, choose one study and record its GEO accession and what was measured.
options.caution: Studies may use different conditions or species; comparing them requires care.

options.label: Try a virtual cell experiment
options.why: PhysiCell is open-source software for simulating cells and their interactions.
options.action: Explore the official examples and identify what a model assumes before changing a setting.
options.caution: A simulation is only as good as its inputs and validation; software setup may require a computer.

choices.label: I want to help research
choices.sub: Check a source, suggest a tool, or share a finding.

options.label: Suggest a source or fix an error
options.why: A well-documented correction improves the Resource Center for every visitor.
options.action: Find a resource or citation that needs attention. Submit only its public URL, what is wrong, and how to verify it.
options.caution: Do not include personal health details in GitHub Issues; they are publicly visible.
options.special_label: Choose a safe way to contribute

options.label: Try reproducing a published result
options.why: Galaxy's free, guided lessons teach how to follow reproducible bioinformatics procedures.
options.action: Choose a beginner tutorial, complete one activity and record its lesson URL and exact result.
options.caution: Training data are not patient data. Reproducing a tutorial is not a new medical discovery.
